verses.note: Scripture opens without an argument for God's existence. It introduces him by what he does, which is how the whole Bible will go on to make him known.

God reveals himself by a name that stresses his power at the moment Abram's body and Sarai's are past hope. The command comes from the same God who will do the impossible, so obedience rests on who he is.

Abraham names God by what the chapter has shown: a God who kept a promise across twenty-five years and will keep it for generations yet unborn. The title fits a man who owns one well and expects an everlasting inheritance.

God does not answer Moses' sense of inadequacy by building up his confidence but by promising his own presence. The pattern returns in the calls of Gideon (Judges 6:15-16) and Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:6-8), and Jesus' last words in Matthew promise the same presence (Matthew 28:20).
Pharaoh's refusal to know the LORD is the question the plagues answer. God makes himself known not by argument but by acts in history, and the goal is that both Israel and Egypt will know who he is.

God makes himself known progressively. The patriarchs knew him as the God who promised; Israel will know him as the God who keeps the promise. The verse teaches that knowing God's name means knowing his character through what he does.
The command presupposes that the God who spoke in verse 2 is unique in claim and in fact. Deuteronomy 6:4 and Isaiah 45:5 later state openly what this command implies: there is no other.
The verse defines Israel's God by name (YHWH) and by relationship (‘our God’) before any attribute. Whatever the exact grouping of the words, it excludes every rival and claims Israel wholly for him.
David's praise does not stop at the gift but moves to the giver. The confession of God's uniqueness is grounded in what he has done, not in speculation.
God is confessed not only as the source of good things but as the good itself. The psalm's later joys (verses 5-11) all follow from this identification.

God's love for Israel is ‘of perpetuity’, older than their sin and outlasting their exile. The verse grounds the promise of return not in Israel's repentance, which comes later in the chapter (verses 18-19), but in a love already in place.

The Old Testament rarely calls God Father, and when it does, as here, the word carries covenant commitment and care for the weak. The father who leads the blind and the lame on a level road is the background for the New Testament's confidence in God as Father.

This verse is one of the Old Testament's clearest windows into God's heart. God speaks against sin and is still moved for the sinner; judgment and compassion are not two moods that alternate but two things true at once. Hosea 11:8 says the same of Ephraim, and Jesus' father running to his returning son (Luke 15:20) stands in this line.

The Ancient of Days is not described as a warrior but as a judge, aged, pure, and surrounded by fire. Against beasts that are new, loud, and violent, God is presented as the one who was there before all of them. White and fire together mean purity and consuming holiness (Deuteronomy 4:24).

The scribes' objection rests on a true premise: forgiveness belongs to the one who is sinned against, and every sin is finally against God (Psalm 51:4). Matthew does not dispute the premise; the story turns on who Jesus is.

In Jonah the sailors' great fear is directed to the LORD, who calmed the sea. Mark uses the same words for the disciples' fear of Jesus. The question "Who is this?" is left open, but the Scriptures behind the story point to only one answer.

Jesus affirms Israel's confession that God is one, and the love it commands is total. The church has never seen the doctrine of the Trinity as a departure from the Shema; Paul reworked the confession itself to include Jesus as the one Lord (1 Corinthians 8:6).
The verse reveals God as the Most High who is kind to the evil. His goodness is not a reward for merit but the ground of all grace (compare Romans 2:4; Matthew 5:45).

The comparison assumes that God is not a trickster. A request made to him in need will not be answered with something that harms, which grounds the believer's trust when the answer is not the one expected.
Jesus pictures God's search through a woman sweeping her house as readily as through a shepherd or a father. The seeking belongs to God's character, not to any one image of him.
The father who runs is Jesus' picture of the God he represents. He is neither indifferent to the son's sin nor waiting to punish it; he is watching for the son to come home.

The father goes out to both sons. God's seeking love reaches the resentful and religious as surely as the reckless, and the parable pictures him pleading with the one who stands outside the celebration.

The phrase the spies use insincerely describes God himself, who shows no partiality (Deuteronomy 10:17, Acts 10:34). Their flattery unwittingly identifies Jesus' teaching with God's own impartial justice.

The oneness of God is not only a claim about how many gods exist but about God's universal claim on all peoples. If there is one God, there is one way into his favor for all, which is grace received by faith.

Paul appeals to the oneness of God, the heart of Israel's confession. The promise rests on God alone, and because God is one, he is the God of all nations (Romans 3:29-30), which is where Paul's argument is heading.
God is the builder of everything. By placing Jesus on the builder's side of the comparison, the verses imply what chapter 1 said openly: the Son shares in the work that belongs to God alone.
